# What Is a Clarification? Estimating Model-Dependent Input Ambiguity

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#circleclar)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20052v1) · arXiv:2610.20052v1, 14 October 2026

**Reading coverage:** All 26 PDF pages, including proof, curation examples, sensitivity analyses, content-aware policy criteria, and all QA/SQL generation and judging prompts in Appendices A-E. Figure 4 visually inspected.

## Research question

Separate ambiguity admitted by an input from valid answers accessible to a particular model.

## Method

Enumerates candidate answers, generates an answer-conditioned clarification for each, and retains candidates consistently recovered when re-answering. The formal clarification-answer bijection assumes faithful, unique clarifications exist for every valid answer.

## Evaluation

Four models on 1,000 AmbigQA questions, 100 curated AmbigQA-HQ questions and 96 ambiguous AMBROSIA requests. SQL uses five enumerations and five recoveries; GPT-5.4-mini groups and judges semantic equivalence. Model-specific references are also recovery-filtered.

## What the results support

Set-F1 leads in seven of twelve model/dataset settings, including two of four SQL settings. Filtering chiefly improves precision at some recall cost. Answer/clarify/abstain and ambiguity-detection experiments are QA-only.

## Limits and qualifications

Cycle consistency can preserve factual errors; missed proposals cannot be recovered. Reference construction shares the recovery criterion and semantic judge with the estimator. The policy labels ANSWER when only one interpretation is model-accessible, even if the world admits others; this is not a user-intent safety guarantee.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Offers a model-dependent ambiguity estimator, with direct SQL answer-set evidence but no SQL dialogue-policy or end-user validation.
